title: Proactive heartbeat federation and token-weighted shedding to stabilize multi-region autoscaling
creator: Priya Patel
description:
Background:
Recent cross-region incident (2026-01-29) exposed a failure mode where rapid traffic reweighting and cold-started replicas in us-east-1 caused autoscaler thrash, regional failover loops, and SLO violations for 95th latency. Existing readiness/liveness probes are binary and locally scoped, which allowed transient errors to be interpreted as persistent unhealthy signals during inter-region handoffs.

Goal:
Design and ship a federated synthetic-heartbeat architecture plus a token-weighted load-shedding policy and an autoscaler cooldown protocol that together reduce autoscaler thrashing, maintain global SLOs during regional failover, and provide observable signals for coordinated rollback. Success criteria: reduce multi-region failover-induced SLO breaches by >= 80% in canary traffic; reduce autoscaler churn (scale events/min) during failover by >= 60%; no measurable increase in steady-state latency for non-degraded regions.

Proposed approach (high level):
1) Heartbeat federation: each region emits a lightweight synthetic heartbeat stream to a small set of peer regions (TLS, authenticated). Heartbeats include: region ID, replica count, moving-average 99th latency, token-weighted backlog estimate, and a small monotonic nonce. These are compact datapoints used only for coordination (not user data).
2) Readiness smoothing: replace strict binary readiness gating used by the global routing controller with a short-term EWMA of remote heartbeats and local probe outcomes. The controller requires a stable window (configurable: 3–10s) before marking a region unhealthy for routing decisions.
3) Token-weighted shedding: when a region is entering degraded state, apply a soft shedding policy that prefers shedding non-realtime token classes (batch/low-priority embeddings) first. Shed decisions are token-aware at the routing layer using our existing cost/latency annotations.
4) Autoscaler cooldown handshake: when heartbeats indicate failover activity, autoscaler controllers honor a cross-region cooldown handshake: inbound scale-downs are delayed for a short, configurable period while scale-ups are rate-limited to prevent overshoot. Cooldown policy is symmetric and token-aware.
5) Observability and safety: build dashboards and SLO monitors that combine local probe trends and remote heartbeat deltas. Expose an emergency abort flag that the on-call can flip to immediately disable federation and revert to current conservative behavior.

Experiments and rollout: 
- Phase A (lab): simulation harness using historical traffic replay (see artifact link) to validate EWMA window parameters and shedding thresholds.
- Phase B (canary): route 5% of cross-region failover candidate traffic through federation with read-only monitors (no actual shedding) for 48 hours.
- Phase C (soft rollout): enable shedding and cooldown in canary region pair for 7 days, observe metrics, increment to 25% then 50%.
- Phase D (global): full enable with per-customer opt-out flag and emergency abort.

Monitoring and success metrics: 
- SLO windows: 95th and 99th generation latency, SLO error budget burn during failover windows.
- Autoscaler churn: number of replica scale events per minute (target: -60% during failover vs baseline).
- Shed effectiveness: fraction of low-priority tokens successfully shed vs total degraded traffic.
- Safety: no new increase in error rate for high-priority tokens.

Implementation notes: 
- Security: heartbeats travel over mTLS authenticated channels; they contain no customer payloads. KMS keys to be used for service identities.
- Backwards compatibility: controllers fallback to legacy behavior if federation handshakes fail.
- Config surface: global flags and per-customer overrides in console; sensible defaults for EWMA half-life, cooldown windows, and shedding thresholds.

Trade-offs and risks: 
- Complexity vs reliability: federation adds cross-region coupling; mitigated by conservative defaults and emergency abort path.
- Edge cases: clock skew and packet loss could bias EWMA; use nonce and sequence checks and conservative timeouts.
- Regulatory: cross-region heartbeat metadata must be filtered for customers who opted into region isolation; provide an opt-out.

Artifacts and links: 
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Heartbeat+Federation+Design
- Simulation harness: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/heartbeat-sim-2026.zip
- Draft PR (controller): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/12834
- Dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/heartbeat-federation-canary

Rollout plan and rollback: 
- Canary-level feature flag control via console; rollout manager to increment by percentage with automated guardrails.
- Rollback: flip abort flag, disable shedding, and allow immediate reconciliation to pre-federation autoscaler parameters.

Open questions: 
- Optimal EWMA window lengths vs observed failover durations (need lab runs).
- Shedding policy fairness across tenants in dedicated pools.
- How to integrate with Dedicated reserved-capacity SLAs (must not autoreduce reserved replicas).

Next steps: 
- Finish controller PoC and run simulation (owners: Connor Lee, Aisha Khan).
- PR for observability metrics (owner: Miguel Ortega).
- Schedule on-call runbook update and tabletop for multi-region failover with federation (owner: Priya Patel).
